title: Average rate of change of a position function
stem: A particle moves along a line with position s(t) = t³ − 2t meters at time t seconds. What is the average rate of change of s over the interval −1 ≤ t ≤ 2, in meters per second?

wrong.rationale: Evaluates the function at the length of the interval instead of forming the difference quotient: 2 − (−1) = 3, and s(3) = 27 − 6 = 21.
Subtracts the outputs in the wrong order but divides by the interval length in the usual order: [s(−1) − s(2)]/(2 − (−1)) = (1 − 4)/3 = −1.
wrong.error_pattern: reversed order of subtraction in numerator

wrong.rationale: Finds the change in output, s(2) − s(−1) = 4 − 1 = 3, and forgets to divide by the change in input, 3.

change_note: New context (position function), cubic with negative left endpoint; distractors recomputed.

title: Average rate of change from a table
stem: The population N(t) of a town, in thousands, t years after 2000 is recorded in the table: N(0) = 10, N(2) = 18, N(4) = 29, N(6) = 42. What is the average rate of change of the population from t = 2 to t = 6, in thousands of people per year?

correct.rationale: The average rate of change is [N(6) − N(2)]/(6 − 2) = (42 − 18)/4 = 24/4 = 6.

wrong.rationale: Computes only the change in output, 42 − 18 = 24, and does not divide by the 4-year change in input.
Averages the two endpoint values, (18 + 42)/2 = 30, instead of dividing the change in output by the change in input.
Divides the change in output by the sum of the inputs instead of their difference: 24/(6 + 2) = 3.

change_note: Function given as a table of data in a population context; different skill entry (read values, then secant slope).

title: Average rate of change of a rational function
stem: A 6-mile trip takes r(x) = 6/x hours when driven at a constant speed of x miles per hour. What is the average rate of change of r as the speed x increases from 2 to 6 miles per hour, in hours per (mile per hour)?

correct.rationale: r(2) = 3 and r(6) = 1, so the average rate of change is (1 − 3)/(6 − 2) = −2/4 = −1/2.

wrong.rationale: Subtracts the outputs in the wrong order, (r(2) − r(6)), giving (3 − 1)/(6 − 2) = 1/2 with the wrong sign.
wrong.error_pattern: reversed order of subtraction in numerator

wrong.rationale: Finds the change in output, 1 − 3 = −2, and does not divide by the change in input, 4.
Evaluates r at the change in input, 6 − 2 = 4: r(4) = 6/4 = 3/2.

change_note: Rational function in a speed/time context; non-integer answer with negative sign.

title: End behavior of an even-degree polynomial
stem: Which statement describes the end behavior of the polynomial function P(x) = 3x⁴ − 5x³ + x?

correct.text: The graph rises on both the left and the right
correct.rationale: The leading term 3x⁴ has even degree and a positive coefficient, so P(x) → ∞ as x → −∞ and as x → ∞.

wrong.text: The graph falls on both the left and the right
wrong.rationale: Treats the leading coefficient 3 as if it were negative; for an even degree this is the pattern of a negative leading coefficient, not 3x⁴.

wrong.text: The graph falls on the left and rises on the right
wrong.rationale: This is the pattern of an odd degree with a positive leading coefficient. The degree here is 4, which is even, so both ends point the same direction.

wrong.text: The graph rises on the left and falls on the right
wrong.rationale: This is the pattern of an odd-degree polynomial with a negative leading coefficient; the degree here is 4 and the leading coefficient is positive.

change_note: Even degree, positive coefficient; choices reworded in words rather than limit notation.

title: End behavior from a product of factors
stem: The polynomial function R(x) = (1 − x²)(x² + 4) is written as a product of two factors. Which statement describes its end behavior?

correct.text: The graph falls on both the left and the right
correct.rationale: Multiplying leading terms gives (−x²)(x²) = −x⁴, so R has even degree 4 and a negative leading coefficient (R(x) = −x⁴ − 3x² + 4); both ends fall.

wrong.text: The graph rises on both the left and the right
wrong.rationale: Reads the factor 1 − x² as if its leading term were +x², obtaining x²·x² = x⁴ with a positive coefficient; the leading term is actually −x².
wrong.error_pattern: ignores negative sign of leading term of a factor

wrong.text: The graph falls on the left and rises on the right
wrong.rationale: Treats the function as odd-degree. Expanding gives R(x) = −x⁴ − 3x² + 4, whose degree is 4 (even), so the ends point the same direction.

wrong.text: The graph rises on the left and falls on the right
wrong.rationale: Treats the degree as odd with a negative leading coefficient; the degree is 2 + 2 = 4, so both ends fall.

change_note: End behavior must be found from factored form with a negative leading term hidden in a factor.

title: End behavior of an odd-degree polynomial
stem: Let S(x) = 4x⁷ − x⁶ + 9. Which statement correctly describes the behavior of the graph of S for inputs of very large magnitude?

correct.text: It falls on the left and rises on the right
correct.rationale: The dominant term is 4x⁷, with odd degree and positive coefficient, so S(x) → −∞ as x → −∞ and S(x) → ∞ as x → ∞.

wrong.text: It rises on both the left and the right
wrong.rationale: Treats the degree 7 as even, as in a positive even-degree polynomial; but 4x⁷ is negative when x is a large negative number.

wrong.text: It falls on both the left and the right
wrong.rationale: Uses the second term, −x⁶ (even degree, negative coefficient), as the dominant term; the term with the highest degree is 4x⁷.
wrong.error_pattern: uses wrong term as leading term

wrong.text: It rises on the left and falls on the right
wrong.rationale: Reverses the pattern, as would happen for a negative leading coefficient. The leading coefficient of 4x⁷ is positive.

change_note: Odd degree, positive leading coefficient, with a distracting even-degree second term.

title: Identify a hole in a rational function
stem: Which statement describes the discontinuity of the rational function R(x) = (x² − x − 12)/(x − 4)?

correct.rationale: Factoring gives (x − 4)(x + 3)/(x − 4). The factor x − 4 cancels, leaving x + 3 for x ≠ 4, so the hole is at x = 4 with y = 4 + 3 = 7.

wrong.rationale: The factor x − 4 appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels, so the discontinuity is removable (a hole), not an asymptote.
Substitutes x = 4 into the original numerator, 16 − 4 − 12 = 0, to get the y-coordinate; the y-coordinate of a hole comes from the simplified function x + 3, which gives 7.
Places the hole at the zero of the remaining factor x + 3. That gives the x-intercept; the hole is at the canceled factor's zero, x = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses remaining zero with canceled factor

change_note: Different polynomial (cancelation with x−4), question framed as describing the discontinuity.

title: Hole and asymptote together
stem: Which statement is true about the graph of g(x) = (x² − 4)/((x − 2)(x + 5))?

correct.text: It has a hole at (2, 4/7) and a vertical asymptote at x = −5
correct.rationale: Since x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), the factor x − 2 cancels, leaving (x + 2)/(x + 5) for x ≠ 2. The hole is at x = 2 with y = (2 + 2)/(2 + 5) = 4/7, and x = −5 remains a vertical asymptote.

wrong.text: It has a hole at (2, 0) and a vertical asymptote at x = −5
wrong.rationale: Gets the right locations but takes the y-coordinate from the original numerator, 2² − 4 = 0; the simplified function gives (2 + 2)/(2 + 5) = 4/7.

wrong.text: It has a vertical asymptote at x = 2 and a hole at x = −5
wrong.rationale: Reverses the roles: the factor x − 2 cancels, so x = 2 is the hole, while x + 5 stays in the denominator, so x = −5 is the asymptote.

wrong.text: It has vertical asymptotes at x = 2 and at x = −5
wrong.rationale: Treats every zero of the denominator as an asymptote without checking for cancelation; x − 2 cancels with the factor in x² − 4.

change_note: Both a hole and a vertical asymptote in one function; requires y-value of the hole.

title: Hole in a quotient with a cubic
stem: The function h(x) = (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) is not defined at x = 2. Which statement describes its graph near x = 2?

correct.rationale: Since x³ − 8 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4), h(x) = x² + 2x + 4 for x ≠ 2, and the hole is at (2, 4 + 4 + 4) = (2, 12).

wrong.rationale: The factor x − 2 divides the numerator exactly, so it cancels and the discontinuity is removable rather than an asymptote.
Uses the numerator's value at x = 2, 2³ − 8 = 0, as the y-coordinate; the y-coordinate comes from the simplified expression x² + 2x + 4, which equals 12 at x = 2.
Divides only the leading term, x³ ÷ x = x², and discards the rest of the quotient, 2x + 4; then evaluates x² at 2 to get 4.

change_note: Difference of cubes requires polynomial division/factoring; hole y-value is not integer-trivial.

title: Crossing versus touching from multiplicities
stem: The polynomial P(x) = (x + 2)³(x − 5)²(x − 1) has real zeros at −2, 5, and 1. At which of these zeros does the graph of P cross the x-axis rather than touch it and turn around?

correct.rationale: The zero −2 has multiplicity 3 (odd) and the zero 1 has multiplicity 1 (odd), so the graph crosses at both. The zero 5 has multiplicity 2 (even), so the graph touches and turns.

wrong.rationale: Reverses the parity rule: the zero 5 has even multiplicity 2, so the graph touches and turns there rather than crossing.
Counts only a multiplicity of exactly 1 as a crossing. Any odd multiplicity crosses, so the zero −2 (multiplicity 3) is also a crossing.
Ignores multiplicity and assumes the graph crosses at every zero; at 5 (multiplicity 2) it touches and turns.

change_note: Factored polynomial with three zeros and multiplicity 3; asks which zeros are crossings.

title: Choose a polynomial from graph behavior
stem: A polynomial function touches the x-axis and turns at x = 3, crosses the x-axis at x = −2, and has no other x-intercepts. Which of the following could be its equation?

correct.rationale: The factor (x − 3)² gives an even multiplicity at 3, so the graph touches and turns there; (x + 2) has multiplicity 1, so the graph crosses at −2.

wrong.rationale: Swaps the multiplicities: this graph crosses at 3 (multiplicity 1) and touches at −2 (multiplicity 2).
Writes the factors with the signs reversed, so the zeros are −3 and 2 instead of 3 and −2.
wrong.error_pattern: sign error when writing factors from zeros

wrong.rationale: Both zeros have multiplicity 1, so the graph crosses at both 3 and −2; it does not touch and turn at 3.

change_note: Construct an equation from described graph behavior rather than interpret a given factored form.

title: Least possible degree from behavior
stem: The graph of a polynomial function touches the x-axis and turns at x = −1, and crosses the x-axis at x = 2 and at x = 4. What is the least possible degree of the polynomial?

correct.rationale: The touch at −1 requires an even multiplicity, at least 2. Each crossing requires an odd multiplicity, at least 1. The least degree is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

wrong.rationale: Counts one for each of the three zeros, as if every zero had multiplicity 1; but a zero where the graph touches and turns needs an even multiplicity, at least 2.
Assigns the touching zero an odd multiplicity of 3, giving 3 + 1 + 1 = 5; a touch needs an even multiplicity, and the least even multiplicity is 2.
wrong.error_pattern: uses odd multiplicity for touch zero

wrong.rationale: Gives every zero multiplicity 2: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. A crossing needs an odd multiplicity, and 1 is the least.

change_note: Reasoning about least degree from touch/cross behavior at three zeros.

title: Caution with a quadratic model
stem: A quadratic function h was fit to measurements of a ball's height taken for times between t = 0.5 and t = 3.5 seconds. Which use of the model should be treated with the most caution?

correct.text: Estimating the height at t = 12 seconds
correct.rationale: t = 12 is far outside the measured interval 0.5 ≤ t ≤ 3.5. Extrapolating that far assumes the fitted pattern continues, which the data cannot support.

wrong.text: Estimating the height at t = 2 seconds
wrong.rationale: t = 2 lies inside the measured interval, so this is interpolation.

wrong.text: Evaluating the model at t = 3.5 seconds
wrong.rationale: t = 3.5 is the last measured time, so it is within the data domain.

wrong.text: Comparing the model's heights at t = 1 and t = 3
wrong.rationale: Both inputs lie inside the measured interval, so the comparison is based on interpolated values.

change_note: Physical context (ball), quadratic model, non-integer domain endpoints.

title: Caution with an exponential revenue model
stem: An exponential function was fit to a company's yearly revenue for the years 2016 through 2022. Which prediction from the model is the least reliable?

correct.rationale: 2040 is 18 years past the last data year, 2022. Such a prediction extrapolates far beyond the data, and the exponential pattern may not continue.

wrong.rationale: 2019 lies between 2016 and 2022, so it is inside the data domain.
2022 is the last year of the data, so it is not beyond the observed domain.
Mid-2018 falls between data years 2016 and 2022, so this is interpolation.

change_note: Different function family (exponential) and a calendar-year context.

title: Evaluating a claim about model reliability
stem: A polynomial model P(t) was fit to data collected for 5 ≤ t ≤ 25. A student claims the prediction P(40) is just as trustworthy as the prediction P(15). Which response is best?

correct.text: The claim is incorrect, because 40 is far outside the data interval, so the pattern may not continue there
correct.rationale: The input 40 is beyond the observed values 5 ≤ t ≤ 25, so P(40) is an extrapolation, while P(15) is an interpolation inside the data.

wrong.text: The claim is correct, because a model that fits the data well fits at every input
wrong.rationale: A good fit on the observed interval says nothing certain about inputs beyond it; P(40) is outside 5 ≤ t ≤ 25.

wrong.text: The claim is incorrect, because P(15) lies inside the data and is therefore less reliable
wrong.rationale: Reverses the idea of reliability: interpolating inside the observed interval is more trustworthy than extrapolating beyond it.

wrong.text: The claim is correct, because polynomial models are valid for all real inputs
wrong.rationale: A polynomial can be evaluated at any real input, but that does not mean it models the situation there; 40 lies outside 5 ≤ t ≤ 25.

change_note: Conceptual evaluation of a claim rather than choosing a prediction.

title: Composition of linear and quadratic
stem: Let f(x) = 3x + 2 and g(x) = x² − 1. Which expression equals (f∘g)(x)?

wrong.rationale: Computes g(f(x)) = (3x + 2)² − 1 = 9x² + 12x + 3, reversing the order of composition.
Adds the functions, (3x + 2) + (x² − 1) = x² + 3x + 1, instead of composing them.
Multiplies the functions, (3x + 2)(x² − 1) = 3x³ + 2x² − 3x − 2, instead of composing them.

change_note: Order of composition is f∘g (seed was g∘f); different functions and distractor types.

title: Composition involving a square root
stem: Let f(x) = √(x + 5) and g(x) = x² − 4. Which expression equals (f∘g)(x)?

wrong.rationale: Computes g(f(x)) = (√(x + 5))² − 4 = x + 1, reversing the order of composition.
Applies the +5 after the square root instead of inside it: √(x² − 4) + 5.
Adds f(x) and g(x), √(x + 5) + (x² − 4), instead of composing them.

change_note: Radical function composition with domain-neutral expressions.

title: Evaluate a composition with an exponential
stem: Let f(x) = 2^x and g(x) = x² − 5. What is the value of (g∘f)(3)?

wrong.rationale: Computes (f∘g)(3) instead: g(3) = 9 − 5 = 4 and f(4) = 2⁴ = 16, reversing the order of composition.
Adds the function values, f(3) + g(3) = 8 + 4 = 12, instead of composing.
Squares f(3) = 8 to get 64 but forgets to subtract 5 in g(8) = 64 − 5.

change_note: Numerical evaluation of a composition with an exponential inner function.

title: Equal-degree rational end behavior
stem: A student is checking what happens to the rational function Q(x) = (2x² − 3x + 1)/(x² + 4) when x grows very large and positive. Comparing the leading terms of numerator and denominator, the right-end behavior of Q is closest to which of the following descriptions?

correct.rationale: The numerator and denominator both have degree 2, so for large x the function behaves like the ratio of the leading coefficients, 2/1 = 2.

wrong.rationale: A limit of 0 would require the denominator's degree to exceed the numerator's. Here both degrees are 2.
Inverts the ratio of leading coefficients, 1/2, instead of numerator over denominator, 2/1.
Keeps only the numerator's leading term 2x² and ignores the denominator x², which should divide it to leave 2.

change_note: Equal degree case (seed was slant); different coefficients.

title: Slant-type end behavior with coefficients
stem: For R(x) = (x + 3)(2x − 1)(x − 4)/(x² + 1), the right-end behavior is closest to

correct.rationale: The numerator has degree 3 with leading coefficient 1·2·1 = 2, and the denominator has degree 2 with leading coefficient 1. So R(x) behaves like 2x³/x² = 2x.

wrong.rationale: Leaves out the coefficient 2 from the factor 2x − 1, using 1 as the numerator's leading coefficient.
Applies the equal-degree rule using only the ratio of leading coefficients, 2/1; but the numerator's degree 3 exceeds the denominator's degree 2.
Divides the leading term 2x³ by x instead of by x², getting 2x²; the denominator's leading term is x².

change_note: Numerator given in factored form; the leading coefficient is not 1.

title: Denominator-dominant rational end behavior
stem: For S(x) = (5x² + 1)/(2x³ − x), the right-end behavior is closest to

correct.rationale: The denominator's degree, 3, exceeds the numerator's degree, 2, so S(x) behaves like 5x²/(2x³) = 5/(2x), which approaches 0. For example S(100) = 50001/1999900 ≈ 0.025.

wrong.rationale: Divides in the wrong direction: it treats 5x²/(2x³) as (5/2)x, but 5x²/(2x³) = 5/(2x).
Uses the ratio of leading coefficients, 5/2, which applies only when numerator and denominator have the same degree.
Reasons that positive leading coefficients make the function grow; but the denominator, of higher degree, grows faster, so S(x) → 0.

change_note: Denominator degree greater than numerator degree (horizontal asymptote y = 0).

title: Model for percent decay
stem: A quantity starts at 250 and decreases by 12% each period. A suitable model for the amount after t periods is

correct.rationale: Each period keeps 100% − 12% = 88% of the amount, so the amount is multiplied by 0.88 each period.

wrong.rationale: Uses the percent decrease, 0.12, as the multiplier; after one period this gives 250(0.12) = 30 rather than 250(0.88) = 220.
Uses the growth factor 1.12, which would model a 12% increase.
Subtracts 0.12 units per period instead of 12% of the current amount; this model is linear, not exponential.

change_note: Decay instead of growth; different start value and rate.

title: Model from a doubling time
stem: A quantity starts at 40 and doubles every 3 years. A suitable model for the amount after t years is

correct.rationale: The amount doubles once every 3 years, so there are t/3 doublings after t years: 40·2^(t/3). At t = 3 this gives 80.

wrong.rationale: Puts the doubling time in the numerator of the exponent; at t = 1 this gives 40·2³ = 320, far more than doubling in 3 years.
Doubles every year instead of every 3 years; at t = 3 this gives 40·8 = 320 rather than 80.
Spreads the 100% increase evenly over 3 years as 1/3 per year; at t = 3 this gives 40(4/3)³ ≈ 94.8, not 80.

change_note: Growth specified by a doubling time instead of a percent rate.

title: Exponential model from table values
stem: The table gives values of a function f: f(0) = 12, f(1) = 18, f(2) = 27, f(3) = 40.5. Which model fits the table exactly?

correct.rationale: Each value is 1.5 times the previous one (18/12 = 27/18 = 40.5/27 = 1.5), and f(0) = 12, so f(t) = 12(1.5)^t.

wrong.rationale: Uses the first difference, 18 − 12 = 6, as a constant rate; but the differences are 6, 9, 13.5, so the growth is not linear. This model gives 24 at t = 2, not 27.
Uses the first difference 6 as the base of the exponential; this gives 72 at t = 1, not 18.
Uses the correct ratio 1.5 but takes the first nonzero-input value 18 as the initial value; at t = 0 this gives 18, not 12.

change_note: Model chosen from a table with common ratio rather than from a verbal rate.

title: Solve a logarithmic equation, base 3
stem: What is the solution of log₃(x + 2) = 4?

correct.rationale: Rewrite in exponential form: x + 2 = 3⁴ = 81, so x = 79.

wrong.rationale: Sets x + 2 equal to the exponent 4 instead of 3⁴, giving x = 4 − 2 = 2.
Rewrites correctly as x + 2 = 81 but adds 2 instead of subtracting it: x = 81 + 2 = 83.
Multiplies the base and the exponent, 3·4 = 12, instead of raising 3 to the 4th power, so x + 2 = 12 and x = 10.

change_note: Base 3, argument x+2, larger answer.

title: Logarithmic equation with a coefficient inside
stem: What is the solution of log₅(2x) = 2?

correct.rationale: Rewrite in exponential form: 2x = 5² = 25, so x = 25/2.

wrong.rationale: Rewrites correctly as 2x = 25 but forgets to divide by 2.
Computes 5² as 5·2 = 10, then divides by 2: x = 10/2 = 5.
Sets 2x equal to the exponent 2 instead of 5², giving x = 1.

change_note: Coefficient on x inside the log; base 5.

title: Logarithmic equation requiring a product and a rejection
stem: What is the solution of log₄(x) + log₄(x − 6) = 2?

correct.rationale: By the product property, log₄(x(x − 6)) = 2, so x(x − 6) = 4² = 16. Then x² − 6x − 16 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 8 or x = −2. Since x = −2 makes log₄(x) undefined, only x = 8 works. Check: log₄ 8 + log₄ 2 = 3/2 + 1/2 = 2.

wrong.rationale: Solves the quadratic correctly but does not reject x = −2, for which log₄(−2) is not defined.
Adds the arguments instead of multiplying them: x + (x − 6) = 16, so 2x − 6 = 16 and x = 11.
Uses the product property but sets the argument equal to the exponent 2: x² − 6x = 2, so x = 3 ± √11, taking the positive root.

change_note: Two logs combined by the product property and an extraneous root, a new situation relative to the single-log seed.

title: Solve an exponential equation in base 3
stem: If 3^(4x + 2) = 20, then x equals

correct.rationale: Taking log base 3 gives 4x + 2 = log₃20. Subtract 2 and then divide by 4: x = (log₃20 − 2)/4.

wrong.rationale: Adds 2 instead of subtracting it when isolating 4x.
Subtracts 2 from the right side but divides only log₃20 by 4, not the whole expression log₃20 − 2.
Divides the argument by 4, giving log₃(20/4) = log₃5, and then subtracts 2; coefficients on x cannot be removed by dividing the argument.

change_note: Base 3 with exponent 4x+2; different constants.

title: Solve with a shift in the exponent
stem: If 7^(x − 4) = 30, then x equals

correct.rationale: Taking log base 7 gives x − 4 = log₇30, so x = 4 + log₇30.

wrong.rationale: Subtracts 4 instead of adding it when isolating x.
Multiplies by 4 instead of adding 4 to both sides.
Adds 4 to the argument, 30 + 4 = 34, instead of adding 4 to the logarithm.

change_note: Shift in the exponent with coefficient 1 on x; base 7.

title: Exponential equation with a coefficient and natural log
stem: If 2e^(3x) = 14, then x equals

correct.rationale: Divide by 2 first: e^(3x) = 7. Then 3x = ln 7, so x = (ln 7)/3.

wrong.rationale: Takes the natural log without first dividing by the coefficient 2: 3x = ln 14, so x = (ln 14)/3.
Removes the 3 by dividing the argument, giving ln(7/3); the 3 multiplies x in the exponent and must come out as a divisor of ln 7.
Multiplies ln 7 by 3 instead of dividing by 3 when solving 3x = ln 7.

change_note: Natural log base and a coefficient in front of the exponential, requiring a first division.
